For the worked starting case, A brings 2 × 3 = 6 kg·m/s and B brings zero. Draw the boundary around both carts. With negligible external impulse, forces between the carts change their individual momenta by equal and opposite amounts, so the system total stays fixed.

Momentum is mass × signed velocity. The before values change when you move a slider.

Explain the mechanism: One shared velocity follows from the total
column2:
Two carts, one momentum total — One shared velocity follows from the total

Sticking gives one final mass mA + mB and one shared velocity v. Conservation gives (mA + mB)v = mA uA + mB uB. Divide the total momentum by total mass. In the worked case, 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. The two green bars have equal signed lengths for every setting.

Conservation alone does not imply sticking. That is the extra collision assumption used here.

Explain the mechanism: Opposite directions cancel in the sum
column2:
Two carts, one momentum total — Opposite directions cancel in the sum

With equal masses and opposite velocities, the contributions are +4 and −4 kg·m/s. Their sum is zero, so the latched pair rests. Neither cart had zero momentum beforehand. Restore any unequal contribution and the pair moves in the direction of the remaining signed total.

Zero total momentum does not mean zero motion or zero kinetic energy before impact.

Two carts, one momentum total — Momentum stays; kinetic energy can change

Which assumption permits conserving momentum for both carts?
column2:
Two carts, one momentum total — Momentum stays; kinetic energy can change

In the worked starting case, kinetic energy falls from 9 J to 6 J even though momentum stays at 6 kg·m/s. Some energy becomes deformation, thermal energy and sound. Total energy is conserved; kinetic energy alone is not. If initial velocities are equal, there is no relative motion and this model predicts no kinetic-energy loss.

Negligible external impulse during the collision

Net external impulse changes total momentum; internal forces cancel in the system sum.

The interaction is idealized; no force-time curve, trajectory or sound is simulated.
